description: Hi! We're passionate about astrophysics, aerospace engineering and science communication. Our core skills include Python, Next.js and orbital mechanics. We're building a team to turn complex NASA data into intuitive, impactful solutions. We are looking for creative UI/UX designers, data enthusiasts and storytellers. Join us if you want to bridge the gap between numbers and the cosmos ( to make the leap possible!!) . Let's build something amazing together!
summary:
On long missions far from Earth, astronauts must spot health changes in themselves, but raw numbers are hard to interpret, especially under stress or fatigue. Jaguarete X is health monitoring software that gathers numerous indicators such as blood pressure, temperature, oxygen and glucose, and presents them in a straightforward dashboard.
Instead of pure charts, the astronaut can select any indicator and our friendly monitoring companion Michi explains each one. After the data is uploaded in the app, Michi analyzes it and, while showing the dashboard, tells them whether they are healthy, what to improve, whether they need food or water, and flags signs of pain, disorientation or nausea. Mental health is as important as our crew’s physical state, so the app includes a section where the astronaut can inform the software about their mood and feelings of loneliness, so it can recommend sleep, exercise and advice to make their stay feel more like home. This helps counter isolation, one of the biggest risks of spaceflight.
Our project detects small changes in our astronauts early, before they become emergencies, and looks after their minds as well as their bodies.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

We built Jaguareté X, a web app that helps astronauts keep track of their health during long missions, like a trip to Mars. It follows each crew member across eight body systems: brain, eyes, breathing, heart, digestion, kidney function, bones and radiation exposure.

Every reading is compared with ranges published by NASA (NASA-STD-3001, the Human Research Program, LSDA and OSDR) and with space weather based on NASA DONKI solar-flare data. Each reading gets one of three labels: good, check or alert. On the main screen there is an X-ray-style body. When you tap a body part, it lights up and shows its data, a trend chart and simple advice on what to do.

We also created Michi, an assistant inspired by the jaguareté, the jaguar native to Paraguay. Michi answers health questions in English and Spanish, explains the readings and can read its answers out loud. It is a rule-based assistant: it matches each question to answers we wrote from NASA sources, so it works completely offline and never makes up medical information.

The app also has:

Self-tests using the screen or camera: an eye check with an Amsler grid, pulse, breathing rate, a reaction-time test and a stand test.

A Play section with workout sessions, a breathing exercise and badges that encourage healthy habits.

Crew and mission management: you can add or remove crew members, each with their own readings, and edit the mission name, description and day.

In this version the sensor readings and solar storms are simulated from published ranges. On a real mission they would come from sensors in the suit and the spacecraft.

What benefits does it have?

The main benefit is that it turns complicated medical data into something anyone on the crew can understand and act on right away. It also works without a connection to Earth. A message can take between 3 and 22 minutes to arrive, so in an emergency the first help has to come from the crew itself. The app also warns early about risks that are specific to space, such as bone and muscle loss, vision changes, kidney stones, radiation and poor sleep. Finally, it takes care of mental health: Michi asks how you feel, and it offers a private talk with the flight psychologist only if you want one.

What is the intended impact?

We want astronauts to have more control over their own health when they are far from Earth and cannot count on real-time support from doctors on the ground. We also think the same idea could help people in isolated places here on Earth, such as research bases or rural communities in Paraguay, where a doctor is not always close by. And it is an educational tool: it shows students how the human body changes in space, using real NASA references.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

Code: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework.

Libraries: Tailwind CSS for the design and Three.js for Michi’s 3D model.

Browser features: the Web Speech API for Michi’s voice, the camera for the self-tests, and local storage to save the crew, the mission and preferences on the device.

NASA data: NASA-STD-3001, Human Research Program reports, LSDA, OSDR (including data from Inspiration4 and the Twins Study) and DONKI for space weather.

Hosting: GitHub for the code and Railway to publish the site.

Hardware: only a laptop or a phone. In the future the app could connect to real sensors in the suit and the spacecraft.

How is our project creative?

Instead of a screen full of numbers, we show a body that lights up where something needs attention, so you understand the problem at a glance. Michi gives the project a friendly and local identity, because the jaguareté is a symbol of Paraguay. And we didn’t want the app to only alert about problems. With the self-tests, breathing exercises, workouts and badges, it also helps the crew take care of themselves every day.

What factors did our team consider?

Distance from Earth: everything had to work offline, including Michi.

Privacy: nothing about an astronaut’s mood is shared without their permission.

Clarity under stress: short messages, three clear levels and one action at a time.

Accessibility: keyboard shortcuts, screen-reader labels, voice output and reduced motion.

Language: we made the app work in both English and Spanish.

Honesty: this is an educational prototype, not a medical device. The values are simulated from published ranges, every area shows its sources, and NASA does not endorse this project.
